text: Link: Source and Credits NavIC (IRNSS) x IRNSS is an independent regional navigation satellite system being developed by India (ISRO). x It is designed to provide accurate position information service to users in India as well as the region extend- ing up to 1500 km from its boundary, which is its primary service area. x IRNSS is a regional and not a global navigation system. x An Extended Service Area lies between primary service area and area enclosed by the rectangle from- 1. Latitude 30 deg South to 50 deg North, 2. Longitude 30 deg East to 130 deg East. x IRNSS will provide two types of services, namely- 1. Standard Positioning Service (SPS) which is provided to all the users and 2. Restricted Service (RS), which is an encrypted service provided only to the authorised users. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 91 x The IRNSS System is expected to provide a position accuracy of better than 20 m in the primary service area. x Some applications of IRNSS are: 9 Terrestrial, Aerial and Marine Navigation 9 Disaster Management 9 Vehicle tracking and fleet management 9 Integration with mobile phones 9 Precise Timing 9 Mapping and Geodetic data capture 9 Terrestrial navigation aid for hikers and travellers 9 Visual and voice navigation for drivers x ISRO has built a total of nine satellites (earlier 7) in the IRNSS series of which eight are currently in orbit. x Three of these satellites are in geostationary orbit (GEO) while the remaining in geosynchronous orbits (GSO) that maintain an inclination of 29° to the equatorial plane. x The IRNSS constellation was named as “NavIC” (Navigation with Indian Constellation). Link: Source and Credits PMF IAS – Learn Smart 92 Basics: https://www.pmfias.com/keplers-laws-satellite-orbits-pslv-gslv/ Additional Reading How Navigation System Works? x Satellite Navigation is based on a global network of satellites that transmit radio signals. x The working of the navigation system is based on the 'trilateration' & ‘triangulation’ principle. x A navigation system device uses data from satellites to locate a specific point on the Earth in a process called trilateration. x To trilaterate, a GPS receiver measures the distances to satellites using radio signals. x Trilateration is similar to triangulation, which measures angles, depicted in this illustration. Link: Source and Credits Triangulation x Triangulation works with line-of-sight. x Triangulation Measures Angles, Not Distance. Trilateration x Three signals put you at one of two points on that circle—and that's usually enough to figure out where you are, because one of the points might be up in the air or in the middle of the ocean. x With four signals, you know your position precisely. x Finding your location this way is called trilateration. x GPS Receivers Use Trilateration. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 93 Link: Source and Credits Link: Source and Credits Private Sector Participation in Space Sector PIB | GS3 > Space Technology PMF IAS – Learn Smart 94 x Context: Government has created Indian National Space, Promotion & Authorization Centre (INSPACe), under Department of Space to encourage the private sector for their participation in Space Sector. IN-SPACe x Private players will also be able to use ISRO infrastructure through INSPACe. x The role of New Space India Limited (NSIL) in the post reformed space sector would be to build launch vehicles, providing launch services, build satellites, providing space-based services, technology transfers, etc. x The broad areas and sectors covered by private companies are- providing materials, mechanical fabrication, electronic fabrication, system development, integration, etc. x IN-SPACe is supposed to be a facilitator, and also a regulator. x It will act as an interface between ISRO and private parties, and assess how best to utilise India’s space resources and increase space-based activities. x IN-SPACe will have a Chairman, technical experts for space activities, Safety expert, experts from Academia and Industries, members from PMO and MEA of Government of India. x IN-SPACe is the second space organisation created by the government in the last two years. x In the 2019 Budget, the government had announced the setting up of a New Space India Limited (NSIL), a public sector company that would serve as a marketing arm of ISRO. x Its main purpose is to market the technologies developed by ISRO and bring it more clients that need space- based services. x That role, incidentally, was already being performed by Antrix Corporation, another PSU working under the Department of Space, and which still exists. About ISRO x The Indian Space Research Organisation is the space agency of the Government of India and has its headquarters in the city of Bangalore (also known as Bengaluru). x Its vision is to "harness space technology for national development while pursuing space science research & planetary exploration". x The Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR) was established by Jawaharlal Nehru under the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) in 1962, with the urging of scientist Vikram Sarabhai recog- nising the need in space research. x INCOSPAR grew and became ISRO in 1969, also under the DAE. x ISRO built India's first satellite, Aryabhata, which was launched by the Soviet Union on 19 April 1975. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 95 Organisation Structure and Facilities x ISRO is managed by the Department of Space (DoS) of the Government of India. DoS itself falls under the authority of the Space Commission and manages the following agencies and institutes: 1. Indian Space Research Organisation 2. Antrix Corporation – The marketing arm of ISRO, Bangalore. 3. Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad. 4. National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL), Gadanki, Andhra pradesh. 5. Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST), Thiruvananthapuram – India's space uni- versity. Indian Missile Systems Ballistic Missile vs. Cruise Missile Ballistic Missiles x Follows a ballistic trajectory to deliver one or more warheads on a predetermined target. x A ballistic trajectory is the path of an object that is launched but has no active propulsion during its actual flight (these weapons are only guided during relatively brief periods of flight). x Consequently, the trajectory is fully determined by a given initial velocity, effects of gravity, air resistance, and motion of the earth (Coriolis Force). PMF IAS – Learn Smart 96 Image Credits: Wikipedia x Shorter range ballistic missiles stay within the Earth's atmosphere. x Longer-ranged intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), are launched on a sub-orbital flight trajectory and spend most of their flight out of the atmosphere. Types of ballistic missiles based on range x Short-range (tactical) ballistic missile (SRBM): Range between 300 km and 1,000 km. x Medium-range (theatre) ballistic missile (MRBM): 1,000 km to 3,500 km. x Intermediate-range (Long-Range) ballistic missile (IRBM or LRBM): 3,500 km and 5,500 km. x Intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM): 5,500 km + Cruise missile x A cruise missile is a guided missile (target has to be pre-set) used against terrestrial targets. x It remains in the atmosphere throughout its flight. x It flies the major portion of its flight path at approximately constant speed. x Cruise missiles are designed to deliver a large warhead over long distances with high precision. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 97 x Modern cruise missiles are capable of travelling at supersonic or high subsonic speeds, are self-navigating, and are able to fly on a non-ballistic, extremely low-altitude trajectory. Types of cruise missiles based on speed x Hypersonic (Mach 5): these missiles would travel at least five times the speed of sound (Mach 5). E.g. BrahMos-II. x Supersonic (Mach 2-3): these missiles travel faster than the speed of sound. E.g. BrahMos. x Subsonic (Mach 0.8): these missiles travel slower than the speed of sound. E.g. Nirbhay. Differences between Ballistic Missile and Cruise Missile Ballastic Missile Cruise Missile x It is propelled only for a brief duration after the launch. x Self-propelled till the end of its flight. x Similar to rocket engine. x Similar to jet engine. x Long range missiles leave the earth’s atmosphere and reenter it. x Flight path is within the earth’s atmosphere. x Low precision as it is unguided for most of its path and its trajectory depends on gravity, air resistance and Coriolis Force. x Hits targets with high precision as it is constantly propelled. x Can have a very long range (300 km to 12,000 km) as there is no fuel requirement after its initial tra- jectory. x The range is small (below 500 km) as it needs to be constantly propelled to hit the target with high precision. x Heavy payload carrying capacity. x Payload capacity is limited. x Can carry multiple payloads (Multiple Inde- pendently targetable Re-entry Vehicle) x Usually carries a single payload. x Developed primarily to carry nuclear warheads. x Developed primarily to carry conventional war- heads. x E.g. BrahMos missiles Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (IGMDP) x IGMDP was conceived by Dr. A P J Abdul Kalam to enable India attain self-sufficiency in missile technology. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 98 x IGMDP was conceived in response to Missile Technology Control Regime that decided to restrict access to any technology that would help India in its missile development program. x To counter the MTCR, the IGMDP team formed a consortium of DRDO laboratories, industries and academic institutions to build these sub-systems, components and materials. Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR) x MTCR an informal grouping established in 1987 by Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United King- dom and the United States to limit the proliferation of missiles and missile technology. x The MTCR seeks to limit the risks of proliferation of weapons of mass destruction (WMD). x MTCR places particular focus on rockets and unmanned aerial vehicles capable of delivering a payload of at least 500 kg to a range of at least 300 km. x The MTCR is not a treaty and does not impose any legally binding obligations. x IGMDP was started in 1983 and completed in March 2012. x Keeping in mind the requirements of various types of missiles by the defence forces, development of five missile systems was taken up. 1. Prithvi: Short-range surface-to-surface ballistic missile (Prithivi means Earth Î Surface to Surface) 2. Agni: Intermediate-range surface-to-surface ballistic missile 3. Trishul: Short-range low-level surface-to-air missile 4. Akash: Medium-range surface-to-air missile (Akash means Sky Î Surface to Air) 5. Nag: Third generation anti-tank missile (Nag means Snake Î Nag slithers like a Snake to hit a tank!) x After its success, Agni missile program was separated from the IGMDP upon realizing its strategic importance. Akash x It has the capability to "neutralize aerial targets like fighter jets, cruise missiles and air-to- surface missiles" as well as ballistic missiles. K-15 Sagarika x It forms the crucial third leg of India’s nuclear deterrent vis-à-vis its submarine-launched ballistic missile (SLBM) capability. x It was subsequently integrated with India’s nuclear-powered Arihant class submarine. Dhanush x It is capable of carrying nuclear warheads. x It carries forward the legacy of the K-15 Sagarika. Shaurya x Surface-to-surface ballistic missile (SSM) variant of the K-15 Sagarika. x The nuclear capability of the missile enhances India’s second strike capability. x It reduces the dependence on the K-15 which was built with Russian assistance. Brahmos Missiles x Brahmos is a multiplatform i.e. it can be launched from land, air, & sea & multi capability missile with pinpoint accuracy that works in both day & night irrespective of the weather conditions. x It has an indigenous booster & air frame sector, along with other sub-systems made within the country. x The supersonic missile is one of the prime precision-strike missiles used by all three forces, the Army, Navy & the Air Force. x BRAHMOS is a joint venture between the Defence Research & Development Organisation of India (DRDO) & the NPOM of Russia. x Brahmos is named on the rivers Brahmaputra & Moskva. x It operates on the "Fire & Forgets" principle i.e it does not require further guidance after launch. x It is supersonic cruise missile. x Brahmos is one of the fastest cruise missile currently operationally deployed with speed of Mach 2.8, which is 3 times more than the speed of sound. x Brahmos is the heaviest weapon to be deployed on Su-30 MKI fighter aircraft, with a weight of 2.5 tonnes. The K Family of Missiles x The K family of missiles are primarily Submarine Launched Ballistic Missiles (SLBMs), which have been developed by DRDO & are named after Dr Kalam. x The development of these naval platform launched missiles began as a step towards completing India’s nuclear triad — the capability of launching nuclear weapons from land, sea & air-based assets. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 103 x Because these missiles are to be launched from submarines, they are lighter than their land-based counter- parts, the Agni missiles which are medium & intercontinental range nuclear capable ballistic missiles. x While K family are primarily submarine-fired missiles to be fired from India’s Arihant class nuclear powered platforms, the land & air variants of some of its members have also been developed by the DRDO. x Shaurya, whose user trial was conducted, is a land variant of short range SLBM K-15 Sagarika, which has a range of at least 750 kilometers. x India has also developed & successfully tested multiple times the K-4 missiles from the family which has a range of 3500 km. x It is reported that more members of K-family — reportedly to have been codenamed K-5 & K-6 — with ranges of 5000 & 6000 km are also under development. The strategic importance of SLBMs x The capability of being able to launch nuclear weapons submarine platforms has great strategic importance in context of achieving a nuclear triad, especially in the light of ‘no first use’ policy of India. x The sea-based underwater nuclear capable assets significantly increase the second-strike capability of a country & thus boosts its nuclear deterrence. x These submarines can not only survive a first strike by the adversary but also can launch a strike in retaliation thus achieving Credible Nuclear Deterrence. Space and Astronomy Related Concepts Asteroids x Asteroids are rocky objects that orbit the Sun, much smaller than planets. x They are also called minor planets. x Asteroids are divided into three classes. 1. First group, those found in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. 2. The second group is that of trojans, which are asteroids that share an orbit with a larger planet. 9 Presence of Jupiter, Neptune, and Mars trojans. 9 In 2011, they reported an Earth trojan as well. 3. The third classification is Near-Earth Asteroids (NEA), which have orbits that pass close by the Earth. 9 Those that cross the Earth’s orbit are called Earth-crossers. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 104 9 More than 10,000 such asteroids are known, out of which over 1,400 are classified as potentially haz- ardous asteroids (PHAs). x Ryugu is also classified as a PHA and was discovered in 1999 and was given the name by the Minor Planet Center in 2015. x It is 300 million kilometres from Earth and it took Hayabusa2 over 42 months to reach it. Hayabusa Mission 2 x The Hayabasu2 mission was launched in December 2014. x The spacecraft was sent on a six-year-long voyage to study the asteroid Ryugu and collect samples to bring back to the Earth. x The spacecraft arrived at the asteroid in mid-2018. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 105 PMF IAS – Learn Smart 106 Closest stars to the Sun x Alpha Centauri is the third brightest star in the sky (4.37 light-years away). x Alpha Centauri is not one star, it is a system of three stars ― Alpha Centauri A & B and Proxima Centauri. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 107 x Alpha Centauri A and Alpha Centauri B are a binary pair, orbiting a common centre of gravity. x Alpha Centauri A is a little more massive than the Sun, & Alpha Centauri B is slightly less massive. x Proxima Centauri is the faint red dwarf star, and it is the closest star to our Sun (4.24 light-years away). x Proxima Centauri has been the nearest star for about 32,000 years. x After 33,000 years from now, the nearest star will be Ross 248. x Alpha Centauri is only visible in the Southern Hemisphere. x In the Northern Hemisphere, the closest visible star is Barnard’s Star, another red dwarf which is too dim just like Proxima Centauri to see with the unaided eye. x The closest star that you can see with the naked eye in the Northern Hemisphere is Sirius (Dog Star). x Sirius is the second brightest star when viewed from the earth, the brightest being the sun. Alpha Centauri Gravitational waves x Gravitational waves are 'ripples' in the fabric of space-time caused by some of the most violent and energetic processes in the Universe. (Spacetime: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sryrZwYguRQ) x Travelling at the speed of light, gravitational waves squeeze and stretch anything in their path. x These ripples travel at the speed of light, carrying with them information about their origins. x Gravitational waves were proposed by Albert Einstein in his General Theory of Relativity. x It was only in 2015, however, that the first gravitational wave was actually detected by LIGO. x Since then, there have been a number of subsequent detections of gravitational waves. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 108 Gravitational waves (NASA) PMF IAS – Learn Smart 109 Source and Credits PMF IAS – Learn Smart 110 x While the processes that generate gravitational waves can be extremely violent and destructive, by the time the waves reach Earth, they are billions of times smaller. Einstein’s theory of general relativity x In 1905, Albert Einstein determined that the laws of physics are the same for all non-accelerating observers and that the speed of light in a vacuum was independent of the motion of all observers. x As a result, he found that space and time were interwoven into a single continuum known as space- time. x Events that occur at the same time for one observer could occur at different times for another. This was the theory of special relativity. x In 1915, Einstein published his theory of general relativity. In it, he determined that massive objects distort space-time, which is felt as gravity. x Gravitational lensing and gravitational waves are strong evidence for Einstein’s theory of general rela- tivity. Gravitational lensing x Light around a massive object, such as a black hole, is bent, causing it to act as a lens for the things that lie behind it. Source: space.com Importance of gravitational waves x The gravitational waves can work as sirens to measure the expansion rate of the universe and to under- stand the origin and the future of the universe. LIGO x The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) was designed to open the field of gravitational-wave astrophysics through the direct detection of gravitational waves predicted by Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 111 Source and Credits LIGO-INDIA x It is the first LIGO LAB outside US. x It aims to create a gravitational-wave detector in India. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 112 x It is a collaboration between LIGO Laboratory and the LIGO-India consortium: Institute of Plasma Re- search, Gandhinagar; IUCAA (Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics), Pune and Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology, Indore. x A site near Aundha Nagnath in the Hingoli district of Maharashtra has been selected. Northern Lights x Aurora is the name given to the luminous glow in the upper atmosphere of the Earth which is produced by charged particles (solar wind) descending from the planet’s magnetosphere. x Northern Lights, also known as aurora borealis, are usually witnessed far up in the polar regions or the high latitude regions of Europe, like in Norway. x While flowing toward Earth, the fast-moving solar wind carries with it the Sun’s magnetic field, which dis- rupts the magnetosphere. x Magnetosphere is the region of space around Earth in which the magnetic field of our planet is dom- inant. x When the Sun’s magnetic field approaches Earth, the protective magnetic field radiating from our planet’s poles deflects the former, thus shielding life on Earth. x However, as this happens, the protective fields couple together to form funnels, through which charged solar wind particles are able to stream down to the poles. x At the north & south poles, the charged particles interact with different gases in the atmosphere, caus- ing a display of light in the sky. x This display, known as an aurora, is seen from the Earth’s high latitude regions (called the auroral oval), & is active all year round. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 113 Visual Explanation > Aurora (Must see) x In the northern part of our globe, the polar lights are called aurora borealis or Northern Lights, & are seen from the US (Alaska), Canada, Iceland, Greenland, Norway, Sweden & Finland. x In the south, they are called aurora australis or southern lights, & are visible from high latitudes in Ant- arctica, Chile, Argentina, New Zealand & Australia. x Generally, the auroral oval is confined to the polar regions. x But occasionally, the oval expands, & the lights become visible at lower latitudes. x This happens during periods of high solar activity, such as the arrival of solar storms. Magnetosphere x The magnetosphere is the region above the ionosphere that is defined by the extent of the Earth’s mag- netic field in space. x It extends several tens of thousands of kilometres into space, protecting the Earth from the charged par- ticles of the solar wind & cosmic rays. x It would otherwise strip away the upper atmosphere, including the ozone layer that protects the Earth from harmful ultraviolet radiation. x Many cosmic rays are kept out of the Solar system by the Sun’s magnetosphere called heliosphere. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 114 Potentially Hazardous Asteroid (PHA) Near-Earth Objects (NEOs) x NEOs are comets and asteroids whose orbits are brought close to the earth’s neighbourhood by the gravi- tational influence of the nearby planets. Asteroids x Asteroids are remnants of planetary formation that circle the Sun in a zone lying between Mars & Jupiter. x The circular chain of asteroids between Mars and Jupiter is called the asteroid belt.
